passage:
Chinmay had stopped at a busy junction when a policeman waved his scooter aside. The officer slid a paper across the seat. "Sign here and pay two thousand now, or the scooter stays." The print was tiny. Chinmay's throat was dry.

"I haven't read this, sir. I won't sign it," Chinmay said evenly. "May I call my cousin Eshaan?"

The officer frowned and said a call would only waste time. "I'll wait," Chinmay replied, and dialled. On speaker, Eshaan said, "Ask for the officer's name and a proper receipt for any fine."

In the end the officer waved Chinmay on with a warning. That night, still shaky, Chinmay wrote down the time and place and filed a complaint on the police portal. Eshaan said, "None of that was your fault."

qa.q: What did the officer say Chinmay must do to keep the scooter?
qa.a: The officer said to sign the paper and pay two thousand now, or the scooter stays.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling while refusing to sign, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Chinmay was frightened but steady: the dry throat shows fear, while the even voice and "I'll wait" show effort to stay calm.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do if a similar demand happens again?
qa.a: Stay calm, not sign anything unread, ask for the officer's name and a receipt, call a relative, and afterwards complain through the official portal.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see the phone call?
qa.a: Eshaan sees a relative who needs practical backup on speaker and wants Chinmay to know none of it was Chinmay's fault.

grounding: An officer pressures Chinmay to pay and sign an unread paper; Chinmay stays calm, refuses, calls family and later complains properly.

passage:
Usha's diary, Saturday.
Got stopped at the traffic signal near the flyover this evening. The officer said my scooter papers were "not valid" and I had to pay two thousand cash, right now, and sign a paper. The paper was in small print and he kept his hand over half of it.
My heart was pounding. For a moment I almost signed just to get away.
But I said, "Sir, I'd like to read it first. Can I have the official challan?" He said it would take long. I said I'd wait. Then I called Dilnaz-didi and put her on speaker. She asked him, very politely, for his name and badge number.
He suddenly said the papers were "okay this time" and waved me on.
When I got home I shook for ten minutes. Then I wrote down the time, place and what he said, and filed a complaint on the traffic department's official grievance portal. Not my fault. Not signing things I can't read.

qa.q: How much cash did the officer ask Usha to pay?
qa.a: Two thousand, in cash, right away.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling during the stop?
qa.a: Usha felt frightened and pressured, heart pounding, and almost signed just to get away.

qa.q: How did Usha handle the coercion?
qa.a: Usha refused to sign without reading, asked for the official challan, called Dilnaz-didi on speaker, noted the details later, and filed an official complaint.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz-didi see the situation over the phone?
qa.a: Dilnaz-didi probably felt worried and protective, and used calm politeness to ask for the officer's name and badge number.

grounding: An officer pressures the protagonist to pay cash and sign an unread paper; they stay calm, refuse to sign blindly, contact family and later complain through proper channels.
